Daniel: [friendly, a little tentative] Hi, Emma. I've just moved into the area, and I'm interested in joining one of your evening classes.
Emma: [helpful, curious] Certainly. Are you looking for something creative?
Daniel: [thoughtful] Yes. I've done a little photography, mostly while travelling, but I've never had any formal training.
Emma: [encouraging] Our beginner photography group could be ideal. We cover composition, exposure and basic lighting.
Daniel: [pleased, curious] That sounds good. When does it meet?
Emma: [clear, matter-of-fact] Wednesday evenings.
Daniel: [confirming, hopeful] Wednesday works. What time does it start?
Emma: [clear, precise] At six thirty, and it finishes at eight fifteen.
Daniel: [curious] And how long does the course run?
Emma: [clear] Six consecutive weeks.
Daniel: [acknowledging] Okay.
Emma: [informative, descriptive] Most sessions are indoors, although there are two outdoor sessions. One is around the riverfront, focusing on reflections and low-light photography, and the other is in the old market district.
Daniel: [pleased] That's good. I was hoping there'd be some practical work.
Emma: [reassuring, informative] There certainly will be. The group has twelve places, and eight people have registered so far.
Daniel: [curious] And what's the fee?
Emma: [clear, matter-of-fact] Eighty-four pounds for all six sessions.
Daniel: [surprised] Eighty-four?
Emma: [confirming, reassuring] Yes, £84. That includes the photography handbook.
Daniel: [accepting] Fine.
Emma: [reassuring, warm] You don't need a professional camera. A smartphone is perfectly acceptable for the first two classes. You can bring a digital camera later if you have one.
Daniel: [pleased] I've got an old digital camera, so I'll probably use that later.
Emma: [warm] That's fine.
Daniel: [decisive, pleased] I'd like to register.
Emma: [warm, satisfied] Great.

Dr. Morris: [warm, welcoming] Good afternoon. I've read your revised proposal. Let's go through the main changes.
Dr. Morris: [curious, recalling] The original proposal focused on household food waste, didn't it?
Adam: [confident] Yes.
Sofia: [matter-of-fact] But household food waste has already been heavily researched.
Dr. Morris: [curious, probing] So why restaurants?
Sofia: [confident, explanatory] Restaurants can provide more measurable data because they keep purchasing and waste records.
Adam: [reflective, conceding] I initially preferred the household study, but the restaurant data should be more consistent.
Dr. Morris: [curious] What's your new research focus?
Adam: [confident, clear] Food-waste reduction practices in medium-sized restaurants, particularly how menu planning affects discarded food.
Dr. Morris: [precise, inquiring] How are you defining medium-sized?
Adam: [informative] We originally considered staff numbers.
Sofia: [explaining] But that's unreliable because many restaurants use part-time workers.
Dr. Morris: [curious] So?
Sofia: [clear, precise] Seating capacity. We're using restaurants with between forty and one hundred and twenty seats.
Dr. Morris: [approving, curious] Good. How will you collect the data?
Sofia: [thoughtful] We originally planned lengthy interviews with restaurant owners.
Adam: [explaining] But they were difficult to arrange during evening service.
Sofia: [confident, informative] So we've replaced those with analysis of weekly purchasing records and waste logs.
Adam: [informative] We'll also record changes to menus.
Dr. Morris: [cautionary] Remember that commercial records can be sensitive.
Adam: [reassuring] We've prepared a confidentiality agreement.
Dr. Morris: [approving, curious] Good. How many restaurants are you hoping to include?
Adam: [confident] Twenty-five originally.
Sofia: [realistic, measured] We've revised that to eighteen to twenty because that's more realistic.
Dr. Morris: [approving, curious] That's sensible. How many are interested?
Adam: [informative] Twelve so far.
Dr. Morris: [curious] And your main outcome measure?
Adam: [clear, explanatory] Percentage reduction in food waste, comparing average weekly waste before and after menu-planning changes.
Dr. Morris: [cautionary, instructive] Be careful about assuming the intervention caused every reduction. Customer numbers, seasonal effects, staffing and supply problems could also affect the results.
Sofia: [confident, reassuring] We've included those variables in the data sheet.
Dr. Morris: [pleased, curious] Excellent. And ethical approval?
Sofia: [informative] The initial paperwork has been submitted. We're waiting for the department's response.
Dr. Morris: [approving] Good.

NARRATOR: [clear, guiding] Section Four. You will hear a university lecturer talking about the science and environmental functions of urban wetlands. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.
NARRATOR: [clear, steady] Now listen and answer Questions 31 to 40.
Test1_Sec4_Full_Voice.mp3
Lecturer: [warm, engaging] Good afternoon.
Lecturer: [confident, informative] Today we're looking at urban wetlands and their role in managing environmental pressures in cities.
Lecturer: [clear, contrasting] Wetlands aren't necessarily remote marshes.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] They can exist beside rivers, around drainage channels, in city parks and on former industrial land.
Lecturer: [confident, organizing] I'll focus on four functions: stormwater management, water-quality improvement, biodiversity, and the challenge of combining ecological functions with public use.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Let's begin with stormwater.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Concrete and asphalt prevent water from soaking into the ground.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] In a natural landscape, some rainfall enters the soil, while vegetation absorbs and slows some of it.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Cities have large impermeable surfaces, so water moves rapidly towards drainage systems.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] When those systems become overwhelmed, flooding can occur.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, emphatic] An important point is that flood risk depends not only on how much rain falls, but also on how quickly water moves.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A wetland can temporarily store rainfall and release it more slowly.
Lecturer: [confident, explanatory] This reduces peak pressure on drainage infrastructure.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Wetlands don't eliminate floodwater, and their storage capacity is limited, so they should be part of a wider drainage system.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Now let's consider water quality.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Urban runoff can contain sediment, nutrients, oils and other pollutants.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] As water passes through dense vegetation, suspended particles can become trapped among plant roots and in wetland soils.
Lecturer: [informative, intrigued] Microorganisms in the sediments also contribute to treatment.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] One important example involves nitrogen.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] Nitrogen is necessary for plant growth, but excessive nitrogen entering rivers and lakes can cause eutrophication.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Eutrophication can stimulate excessive algae growth.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] When large quantities of algae die, microorganisms decompose them and consume oxygen.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] As oxygen levels fall, fish and other aquatic organisms may struggle to survive.
Lecturer: [clear, informative] Wetlands can help remove some nitrogen through microbial processes in waterlogged soils.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, cautionary] Their effectiveness depends on water movement, soil characteristics, temperature and vegetation.
Lecturer: [clear, cautionary] So simply constructing a pond does not automatically create an effective treatment wetland.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Let's move on to biodiversity.
Lecturer: [confident, warm] Urban wetlands can provide habitat for amphibians, insects, birds and aquatic plants.
Lecturer: [informative] For some species, a wetland provides a temporary refuge.
Lecturer: [informative] For others, it can become a breeding site.
Lecturer: [informative] Wetlands can also connect otherwise isolated green spaces.
Lecturer: [informative, intrigued] These connections can act as ecological corridors, allowing animals to move through urban areas.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, transitional] However, wetlands also attract people.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Residents may want walking routes, schools may want educational facilities, and visitors may want viewing platforms.
Lecturer: [balanced, measured] These activities can be compatible with conservation if access is carefully managed.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Heavy foot traffic can compact surrounding soil and affect water movement.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Visitors may also disturb nesting birds.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is why wetlands often include boardwalks, viewing platforms and clearly defined routes.
Lecturer: [clear, informative] A raised boardwalk allows people to experience a wetland while reducing disturbance.
Lecturer: [confident, transitional] There is also an educational benefit.
Lecturer: [reflective] An underground drainage system is difficult for residents to understand.
Lecturer: [delighted, illustrative] A visible wetland allows people to see water being stored and managed.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, cautionary] However, wetlands can sometimes look untidy compared with conventional parks.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Mud, dead vegetation and changing water levels are normal ecological features.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Now let's return to engineering.
Lecturer: [clear, cautionary] Designing an effective urban wetland is not simply a matter of digging a pond.
Lecturer: [informative] Engineers need to consider water depth, seasonal rainfall patterns, soil composition and the surrounding drainage network.
Lecturer: [measured, emphatic] Water levels are particularly important.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] If a wetland remains permanently flooded, some plants may disappear.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] If it dries too frequently, its ability to retain water and support aquatic organisms may be reduced.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] Seasonal variation can therefore be beneficial.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Soil composition is also important.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Highly permeable soil may allow water to disappear too quickly, while impermeable soil can create other drainage problems.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, cautionary] Maintenance is another consideration.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Plants need monitoring, invasive species may need removal, and sediment can accumulate.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Drainage structures can become blocked, while boardwalks and viewing platforms require inspection.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, rhetorical] The important question is whether the wetland can continue performing its intended functions over many years.
Lecturer: [reflective, transitional] There is also a social dimension.
Lecturer: [confident, warm] Urban wetlands can provide recreational and educational spaces.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But excessive recreational use can damage vegetation, disturb wildlife and compact soil.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Successful projects therefore require managed access.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Why are urban wetlands becoming more important?
Lecturer: [measured, forward-looking] One reason is climate change.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] More intense rainfall events can place additional pressure on drainage infrastructure.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] At the same time, urban development reduces the amount of undeveloped land available for natural water storage.
Lecturer: [informative, impressed] A wetland can provide several functions at once: flood storage, water-quality improvement, wildlife habitat and recreation.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But wetlands are not a universal solution.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] They cannot eliminate flood risk or remove every pollutant, and they cannot completely replace conventional drainage infrastructure.
Lecturer: [clear, balanced] Instead, they can form part of a wider green-infrastructure strategy.
Lecturer: [informative] Green infrastructure includes rain gardens, green roofs, permeable surfaces and wetlands.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] The basic principle is to slow water down where possible.
Lecturer: [clear, explanatory] Rather than allowing rainfall to move immediately from roof to pipe to river, planners can create temporary storage areas.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, transitional] Another possibility is converting degraded urban land into wetlands.
Lecturer: [informative] Former industrial sites and unused drainage areas may sometimes be suitable.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, contaminated land creates additional challenges.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Engineers need to determine whether pollutants are present before construction begins.
Lecturer: [clear, informative] This is why urban wetland projects require collaboration.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Hydrologists study water movement.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Ecologists examine habitat and species.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Engineers deal with structures and drainage.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Urban planners consider land use.
Lecturer: [matter-of-fact] Community specialists can help understand how residents will use the site.
Lecturer: [thoughtful, reflective] Success can also be measured in different ways.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] An engineer might examine whether flood pressure has been reduced.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] An ecologist might look at bird or amphibian populations.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] A water-quality scientist might measure nitrogen concentrations.
Lecturer: [warm, illustrative] Residents may simply ask whether the area has become a useful part of their neighbourhood.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] All these perspectives are relevant.
Lecturer: [measured, emphatic] So remember that an urban wetland is not simply a pond.
Lecturer: [confident, clear] It is a managed ecological system involving hydrology, soil, vegetation, microorganisms, wildlife and human behaviour.
Lecturer: [reflective, concluding] Modern planners increasingly view stormwater as something that can be temporarily stored, filtered and incorporated into the landscape.
Lecturer: [reflective, emphatic] That represents an important change in thinking.
Lecturer: [clear, illustrative] Instead of asking only how quickly water can be removed from a city, planners can ask where water can safely remain for a while.
Lecturer: [confident, warm] Cities need infrastructure that can respond to environmental pressures while providing ecological and social benefits.
Lecturer: [clear, concluding] Urban wetlands are one example.
Lecturer: [warm, forward-looking] Next week we'll examine green roofs and their contribution to urban climate adaptation.
Lecturer: [warm, concluding] Please read Chapter Nine before the seminar.
Test1_Sec4_End_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: [calm, concluding, final] That is the end of the Listening test.

Maya: [warm, welcoming] Today I'd like to explain what happens to food waste after residents bring it to our community composting centre. The process begins when food waste arrives from collection points around the neighbourhood. The material is weighed before it enters the processing area. The first stage is marked A on your diagram. This is the collection stage, where organic material is received and recorded. After collection, the waste moves to the sorting station. At this stage, staff remove materials that shouldn't be composted, such as plastic packaging, glass and metal. The sorting stage is marked B. Once the material has been sorted, it moves to a mechanical shredder. This stage, marked C, reduces large pieces of food waste into smaller fragments. Why is that necessary? Smaller pieces provide a more even mixture and make decomposition easier. After shredding, the material moves to the mixing area, marked D. Here, food waste is combined with dry carbon-rich material such as leaves or shredded cardboard. This balance is important because food waste tends to contain a lot of moisture and nitrogen. If the mixture contains too much wet material, it can become compact and unpleasantly anaerobic. If there's too much dry material, decomposition may be slower. The mixed material is then moved into long composting piles. At this point, microorganisms begin breaking down the organic material. The temperature inside the piles can rise considerably because microbial activity releases heat. However, the microorganisms need oxygen. This brings us to the next stage, marked E. Air is introduced into the piles through a simple aeration system. In smaller facilities, workers may turn the material mechanically instead. Either way, the aim is to prevent oxygen levels from becoming too low. The material remains in the active composting area for several weeks. During this period, moisture and temperature are checked regularly. The material doesn't become finished compost immediately. It needs additional time after the most active stage has passed. That later stage is called curing.

Maya: [warm, welcoming] Let's continue with the second half of the process. After the active composting period, the material enters the curing stage. On your diagram, this is marked F. Curing takes place at a lower temperature. During this period, the remaining organic material continues to break down gradually. The compost becomes more stable and develops the dark, crumbly appearance associated with mature compost. Once curing is complete, the material moves to the screening station, marked G. Screening removes larger pieces that have not decomposed fully. These pieces aren't necessarily thrown away. They can often be returned to a new compost pile and processed again. The final material passes through the screen and is collected as finished compost. That final product is marked H. It can be used in community gardens, parks and planting areas. One point worth remembering is that compost quality depends heavily on what enters the system at the beginning. If residents put plastic bags or other unsuitable materials into food-waste containers, staff have to remove them later. That increases labour and can reduce the quality of the final product. Temperature is also important. During the active stage, temperatures may become high enough to destroy many weed seeds and harmful organisms. But the pile must still receive enough oxygen. Too little oxygen can produce unpleasant odours and slow the process. Moisture is equally important. A pile that's too dry may decompose slowly. One that's excessively wet can become compact. Lecturer: [warm, welcoming] Good afternoon.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Today we're going to examine microplastics in freshwater environments.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] When people hear about plastic pollution, they often imagine bottles, bags or other large objects.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But a significant part of the problem involves much smaller pieces known as microplastics.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The term generally refers to plastic particles smaller than five millimetres.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some are manufactured at a small size, while others are created when larger plastic objects gradually break apart.
Lecturer: [intrigued, engaged] Freshwater systems are particularly interesting because rivers and lakes can act both as pathways and temporary storage areas for these particles.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Let's begin with where microplastics come from.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] One source is the breakdown of larger plastic waste.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A bottle exposed to sunlight, heat and physical abrasion can gradually fragment.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The resulting pieces become smaller over time.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Another source is synthetic textiles.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] When clothes made from materials such as polyester are washed, tiny fibres can be released.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] These fibres may enter wastewater systems.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Wastewater treatment plants can remove a large proportion of them, but not necessarily all.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Particles can therefore reach rivers through treated wastewater.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Roads are another source.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Vehicle tyres gradually wear down during driving, producing particles that can accumulate on roads.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Rain can then wash some of this material into drainage systems and eventually into rivers.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So microplastic pollution doesn't come from a single source.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It comes from a combination of household, industrial and transport-related activities.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Once particles enter a river, their movement depends partly on their physical characteristics.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Size is important.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Density is also important.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some plastics are less dense than water and may remain near the surface.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Other particles are denser or become attached to heavier material and sink towards the riverbed.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This means that sampling only the surface water may give an incomplete picture.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Researchers therefore collect samples from different depths and sometimes from sediments.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Sediments are particularly important because particles can accumulate there over long periods.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A river can transport a particle downstream during one period and then deposit it in sediment during another.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Later, changes in water flow may disturb the sediment and release particles again.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This means that freshwater environments can function as temporary storage systems.
Lecturer: [curious, probing] Now, how do scientists detect microplastics?
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] The first step is usually collecting a water or sediment sample.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The sample is then processed in a laboratory.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Large organic material may be removed before the remaining particles are examined.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Visual inspection can sometimes provide useful information, but it isn't always reliable.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A small piece of plastic can resemble natural material.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] For that reason, researchers often use chemical or spectroscopic techniques.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] One common approach is infrared spectroscopy.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The instrument examines how a material interacts with infrared radiation.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Different polymers have characteristic chemical signatures.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Researchers can therefore compare the signature of an unknown particle with reference materials.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This allows them to determine whether a particle is plastic and, in many cases, identify the type of polymer.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Sampling itself creates another challenge.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Plastic materials are present in many laboratories and everyday environments.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] A researcher wearing synthetic clothing, for example, could accidentally introduce fibres into a sample.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is called contamination.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] To reduce the problem, researchers may use cotton laboratory clothing, clean equipment carefully and include blank samples.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] A blank sample contains the laboratory materials and chemicals used in the analysis but does not contain the environmental sample itself.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] If plastic fibres appear in the blank, researchers know that contamination has occurred somewhere in the procedure.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Now let's consider what microplastics do once they're present in freshwater.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The ecological effects are still being investigated.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Small organisms such as zooplankton can ingest particles accidentally.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some fish and aquatic invertebrates may also consume them.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] The concern is not simply that the particles occupy space in an animal's digestive system.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Microplastics may interact with other substances in the environment.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Their surfaces can attract certain pollutants.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, the importance of this process under real environmental conditions is still being studied.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Another question concerns movement through food webs.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If a small organism consumes a particle and is then eaten by a larger organism, the particle may move between trophic levels.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But this does not mean that every particle automatically travels all the way to humans.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The pathway depends on particle characteristics, species behaviour and environmental conditions.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So researchers need to avoid making claims that are stronger than the evidence allows.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Freshwater research is also complicated by seasonal variation.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] During periods of heavy rainfall, river flow can increase substantially.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This may transport particles that had accumulated on land or in drainage systems.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] During dry periods, water movement may be slower and particles may have more opportunity to settle.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Consequently, a sample collected in one month may look very different from one collected several months later.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is one reason long-term monitoring is valuable.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A single sampling event provides a snapshot.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Repeated sampling can reveal patterns.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Researchers may discover that certain locations consistently have higher concentrations than others.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They can then investigate why.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Urban areas may show elevated levels because they contain dense populations, roads, wastewater systems and large quantities of manufactured materials.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But rural areas aren't necessarily free of microplastics.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Agricultural runoff, atmospheric deposition and wastewater can also transport particles into less developed environments.
Lecturer: [curious] What can be done to reduce the problem?
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] The most effective approach is usually to reduce plastic entering the environment in the first place.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Improving waste collection can prevent larger plastic objects from fragmenting.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Better management of textile fibres can also help.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Washing-machine filters are one possible intervention, although their effectiveness depends on design and maintenance.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Wastewater treatment can remove many particles, but improving removal may require additional technologies and energy.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Road runoff presents another challenge.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Drainage systems can sometimes include filters or settling areas that capture particles before they reach rivers.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, these systems themselves require maintenance.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Captured material has to be removed and managed appropriately.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] This illustrates an important principle in environmental management.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Pollution control isn't simply about installing a technology.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The system has to operate effectively over time.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Finally, we need better standardisation.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Different research teams sometimes use different sampling methods, particle-size ranges and laboratory procedures.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] That can make studies difficult to compare.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If researchers use more consistent methods, we can develop a clearer picture of how microplastic concentrations vary between rivers and regions.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So, to conclude, microplastics are not a single type of pollutant with a single source.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They are a diverse collection of small plastic particles produced by many human activities.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Their movement through freshwater depends on characteristics such as size and density, as well as water flow and sediment conditions.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Their ecological effects are still being studied.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] And because contamination can easily occur during research, careful sampling and laboratory procedures are essential.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The broader lesson is that environmental pollution often requires us to look beyond what is immediately visible.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] A river may appear clean while still containing particles that cannot be seen easily.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Understanding those hidden forms of pollution is an important part of modern freshwater science.

Lecturer: [warm, welcoming] Good afternoon.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Today we're going to examine why some urban trees survive heat and drought better than others.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Trees are often presented as a simple solution to urban heat.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They provide shade, reduce surface temperatures and can improve the quality of public spaces.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But planting a tree does not automatically guarantee these benefits.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The tree has to survive.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] And urban environments can be surprisingly difficult places for trees to grow.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Let's begin with water.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] During hot weather, trees lose water through a process called transpiration.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Water moves from the soil through the tree and eventually escapes through tiny openings in the leaves called stomata.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This movement helps cool the tree.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But it also means that a tree can lose substantial amounts of water during a hot, dry period.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] When soil water becomes limited, trees face a problem.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They need to reduce water loss while still maintaining photosynthesis.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] One response is to close their stomata.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] This reduces water loss, but it also limits the entry of carbon dioxide.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] As a result, photosynthesis can decline.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] So a tree cannot simply close its stomata indefinitely.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is one reason drought can have effects that continue even after rainfall returns.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Now consider the urban soil itself.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] In natural forests, soil contains organic material, air spaces and networks of roots and microorganisms.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Urban soil may be very different.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Construction can remove the original topsoil.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Heavy machinery can compact the remaining soil.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Compaction reduces the spaces through which air and water move.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Roots therefore have greater difficulty growing through compacted soil.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] This is especially important near roads and pavements.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] A tree may appear to have plenty of soil around it, but the soil beneath a pavement may be heavily compacted.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Another problem is the size of the available rooting area.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Trees need roots not only for physical support but also to obtain water and nutrients.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A small planting pit may restrict root development.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This can reduce the tree's ability to tolerate drought.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So when urban planners choose tree species, they need to consider the space available underground as well as the appearance of the tree above ground.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Species selection is a major factor in urban tree survival.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Different species have different tolerances to heat, drought, salt and pollution.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some species naturally occur in dry environments and have adaptations that help them conserve water.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Others are adapted to cooler or wetter conditions.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This doesn't mean that drought-tolerant species can survive without water.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It means they may continue functioning for longer under water stress.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Leaf characteristics are also important.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some trees have small leaves, thick leaf surfaces or other features that reduce water loss.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Others may have deep root systems that allow them to access water further below the surface.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Root depth, however, depends partly on soil conditions.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] A genetically drought-tolerant tree cannot fully express its potential if its roots are unable to penetrate the surrounding soil.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Urban heat creates another challenge.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb solar energy and become very hot.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Trees planted beside these surfaces can experience higher temperatures than trees in cooler landscapes.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Buildings can also affect air movement.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] In narrow streets, heat may become trapped.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The amount of available shade therefore matters.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Young trees are particularly vulnerable.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A mature tree may have a large root system and a broad canopy.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A newly planted tree has neither.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] This is why the first few years after planting can be critical.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Regular watering may be necessary while the root system becomes established.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, watering practices need to be carefully designed.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Overwatering can cause its own problems.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If soil remains saturated for long periods, roots may have insufficient oxygen.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The goal is therefore not simply to provide as much water as possible.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It is to provide water when and where the tree needs it.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Mulching can help.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A layer of organic material placed around the base of a tree can reduce evaporation from the soil surface.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It can also moderate soil temperature.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, mulch should not be piled directly against the trunk because this can create other problems.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Another important issue is competition.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Urban trees may share limited soil and water resources with grass, shrubs and other vegetation.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] In some locations, underground utilities also restrict root growth.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] This makes the design of the planting site important.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Rather than treating the tree as an isolated object, planners should consider the entire growing environment.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Tree survival is also connected to climate change.
Lecturer: [delighted, pleased] As heatwaves become more frequent or intense in some regions, species that previously survived comfortably may experience greater stress.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Urban planners therefore need to think about future conditions rather than simply selecting species that perform well under today's climate.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] This is sometimes called climate-resilient planting.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But predictions contain uncertainty.
Lecturer: [confirming] We don't know exactly what conditions every city will experience decades from now.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A sensible strategy is therefore to increase diversity.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If every street contains the same tree species, a disease or environmental stress affecting that species could cause widespread losses.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A mixture of species creates a form of biological insurance.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, diversity needs to be managed carefully.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Not every species is suitable for every location.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some may have invasive characteristics.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Others may damage pavements through aggressive root growth.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Some produce large quantities of pollen or fruit that may create maintenance problems.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So species diversity does not mean choosing species randomly.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It means selecting a range of appropriate species with different characteristics.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] There is also a question of measuring success.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A tree-planting programme might report the number of trees planted.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But that figure tells us very little about long-term performance.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A more useful measure may be the proportion of trees that remain healthy after five or ten years.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Researchers can also measure canopy growth, leaf condition and survival during heatwaves.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] These indicators help distinguish between successful planting and simply planting large numbers of trees.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The benefits of mature urban trees can be substantial.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A large canopy can provide shade over roads, pavements and buildings.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Trees can also influence local microclimates by reducing solar exposure and through evapotranspiration.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But these benefits increase as trees grow.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A programme that replaces dead young trees every few years may never produce the same benefits as a programme that successfully establishes mature trees.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So maintenance is not an optional extra.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It is part of the planting strategy.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] To conclude, successful urban tree planting involves much more than choosing attractive species.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] We need to consider water availability, soil condition, root space, heat exposure, species characteristics and long-term maintenance.

Lecturer: [warm, welcoming] When people think about conserving plants, they often imagine forests, botanical gardens or protected areas.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But there is another form of conservation that happens largely out of sight.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is the preservation of seeds in specialised facilities known as seed banks.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The basic idea is quite simple.
Lecturer: [explaining, adjusting] Instead of keeping every plant alive in the field, scientists collect seeds and store them under controlled conditions.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] If the species later disappears from a particular location, stored seeds may provide material for research or, in some circumstances, for restoring populations.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, seed banking is not simply a matter of putting seeds into a refrigerator.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] The first stage is collection.
Lecturer: [confirming] Scientists need to know exactly where the seeds came from.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They record the location, the plant species and often information about the environment in which the plant was growing.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This information matters because a collection is much more useful when researchers understand its origin.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Two populations of the same species may have adapted to different local conditions, so preserving material from several populations can capture a wider range of genetic characteristics.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] After collection, the seeds are usually cleaned.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Leaves, pieces of fruit and other unwanted material are removed.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The seeds may then be tested to determine whether they are viable.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Viability simply means whether a seed is capable of producing a healthy plant under suitable conditions.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A collection containing thousands of dead seeds would obviously have limited value.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] One common test involves taking a small sample of seeds and attempting to germinate them.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If a high proportion develops normally, researchers can be more confident that the stored collection is in good condition.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] The next challenge is drying.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Many seeds tolerate drying extremely well.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] In fact, reducing their moisture content is one of the key steps in preparing them for long-term storage.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Water inside biological material can contribute to chemical reactions and cellular damage.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] By carefully reducing the amount of moisture, scientists can slow these processes.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But not every seed behaves in the same way.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some seeds are highly sensitive to drying.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] These are sometimes called recalcitrant seeds.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] They may be damaged if their moisture content becomes too low, which makes conventional seed banking difficult.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] For seeds that can tolerate drying, the next stage is usually low-temperature storage.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A seed bank may maintain temperatures well below freezing.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The aim is to slow biological and chemical processes so dramatically that the seeds can remain viable for many years.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] The precise temperature is important, but so is the stability of the storage environment.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Repeated changes in temperature can be harmful.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] For this reason, seed banks use carefully controlled equipment and monitoring systems.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Researchers also need to know how long a particular seed collection is likely to remain viable.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] They cannot simply assume that every species will survive for the same period.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some seeds remain viable for decades, while others deteriorate much more quickly.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is why seed banks periodically conduct germination tests on stored material.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A small sample can be removed and tested to see whether the seeds are still capable of developing.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If viability has fallen below an acceptable level, the seed bank may need to grow new plants and collect fresh seeds.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] This process is sometimes called regeneration.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Regeneration sounds straightforward, but it carries a potential problem.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If scientists grow only a small number of plants, they may accidentally preserve only part of the genetic diversity originally present in the collection.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Imagine a population containing several genetic variants.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] If regeneration is based on just a few plants, some variants may not be represented in the next generation.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] For this reason, scientists try to use sufficiently large populations and carefully managed growing conditions.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Seed banks are therefore not passive storage facilities.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They involve continuing scientific work.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Another important function of seed banks is research.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Stored seeds can help scientists investigate how plants respond to drought, temperature changes or different soil conditions.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Researchers may compare material collected from different environments and look for characteristics associated with survival.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This can become particularly valuable as climate conditions change.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] For example, suppose a plant currently grows successfully in a relatively cool environment.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If temperatures increase over several decades, scientists may want to know whether populations from warmer regions contain characteristics that could help the species adapt.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The stored material can provide an opportunity to investigate that question.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Seed banks can also support agriculture.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Modern crops often have relatively narrow genetic bases because farmers tend to grow varieties with particular desirable characteristics.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Wild relatives and older crop varieties may contain genes associated with resistance to diseases, tolerance of drought or adaptation to poor soils.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Preserving this material gives researchers access to characteristics that may become valuable in the future.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, seed banks cannot replace conservation in natural habitats.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A seed in a freezer is not part of an ecosystem.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It does not interact with insects, fungi, soil organisms or neighbouring plants.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is why conservation scientists often distinguish between ex situ conservation, which takes place outside the natural habitat, and in situ conservation, which protects organisms within their natural environments.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The two approaches can complement one another.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] In situ conservation protects the ecological relationships that make a species part of a functioning ecosystem.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Seed banks provide a backup and a research resource.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] There are also practical limitations.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Not all plant species produce seeds that can be stored conventionally.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some reproduce mainly through other structures, while certain seeds lose viability rapidly under storage conditions.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] For these species, scientists may need alternative conservation techniques, including living collections or the preservation of plant tissue.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Even so, seed banking has become an important part of global plant conservation.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Its greatest value may be that it gives researchers something that natural populations cannot always provide: a preserved record of genetic material from a particular place and time.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But that record is useful only if it is carefully documented, tested and maintained.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] So when we think about a seed bank, we shouldn't imagine a warehouse full of dormant seeds and nothing more.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] We should think of it as a long-term scientific programme involving collection, documentation, testing, storage and, when necessary, regeneration.

Lecturer: [warm, welcoming] Coral reefs are often described as some of the most productive ecosystems in the ocean.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They provide habitat for many species, protect coastlines from waves and support human communities through fishing and tourism.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] But coral reefs are also exposed to disturbance.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A disturbance might be a severe storm, a period of unusually warm water, physical damage from human activity or a disease outbreak.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] After such an event, the important question is not simply how much coral has been lost, but whether the reef can recover.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Recovery is a process rather than a single event.
Lecturer: [clear, transitional] Let's begin with what happens during a major disturbance.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] One of the most visible effects of unusually warm water is coral bleaching.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Corals have a close relationship with microscopic algae living within their tissues.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] These algae provide energy to the coral through photosynthesis.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] When environmental conditions become stressful, particularly when temperatures remain unusually high, corals may lose these algae or expel them.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The coral tissue then becomes pale, revealing the white skeleton beneath.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is called bleaching.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Bleaching does not automatically mean that the coral is dead.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If stressful conditions are relatively short-lived, corals may regain their algae and survive.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The possibility of recovery depends partly on the duration of the stress.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] A short period of high temperature may produce substantial bleaching but still allow many colonies to recover.
Lecturer: [delighted, pleased] Longer periods can cause much greater mortality.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Another factor is the condition of the reef before the disturbance.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A reef that is already affected by pollution, sediment or overfishing may have fewer resources available for recovery.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Once the disturbance has ended, recovery can occur through several mechanisms.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] One is the survival and regrowth of coral colonies that were only partially damaged.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Another is the arrival of new coral larvae.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Corals reproduce in several ways, but many reef-building corals release reproductive cells into the water.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] After fertilisation, developing larvae can be transported by ocean currents.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If these larvae settle successfully on suitable surfaces, they can begin developing into new colonies.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This process is called recruitment.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Recruitment is particularly important after large disturbances because it can introduce new individuals into damaged areas.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] However, settlement does not guarantee survival.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Young corals are vulnerable.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] They compete with algae and other organisms for space, and they can be affected by sediment, predators and changes in water quality.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] This means that the availability of suitable settlement surfaces is another important factor.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Imagine a reef where coral has died but the exposed surface is quickly covered by thick algae.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] A coral larva arriving in that area may struggle to establish itself.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] By contrast, an area with clean, stable surfaces may provide better opportunities for new coral growth.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Herbivorous fish can also influence this process.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] These fish consume algae, helping to prevent algae from dominating available surfaces.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This means that fishing pressure can indirectly affect coral recovery.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] If herbivorous fish are heavily removed, algae may become more abundant, potentially making it harder for young corals to establish.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] This is one reason why reef management is not simply about protecting coral itself.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Maintaining the broader community can improve the conditions required for recovery.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Another factor is water quality.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Sediment entering coastal waters can settle on coral surfaces and interfere with feeding or photosynthesis.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Excess nutrients can also change the balance between corals and algae.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] For this reason, reducing pollution from land can be an important part of reef conservation.
Lecturer: [measured, cautionary] Climate change creates a more difficult challenge.

Lecturer: [warm, welcoming] Trees are one of the most visible forms of urban vegetation, but their contribution to city life goes beyond making streets look attractive.

Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Urban air contains a mixture of gases and particles.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some pollutants come directly from vehicles, industrial activity and heating systems.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Others form through chemical reactions in the atmosphere.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Street trees interact with this polluted air in several ways.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The most familiar mechanism is deposition.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Particles suspended in the air can come into contact with leaves, branches and other plant surfaces.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Some remain attached to those surfaces rather than continuing to move through the atmosphere.
Lecturer: [clear, emphatic] Leaves are particularly important because they provide a large surface area.

Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] The effectiveness of vegetation depends on the pollutant involved, the tree species, the structure of the street and the weather.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Leaf characteristics matter.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Leaves with rough or complex surfaces can capture particles more effectively than very smooth surfaces.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] Fine structures such as hairs can also increase the available surface area.

Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Rain can wash material from leaves onto the ground.

Lecturer: [explaining, adjusting] Instead, some of it has simply been transferred elsewhere.

Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Consider a narrow road surrounded by tall buildings.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Air movement may already be restricted.
Lecturer: [informative, descriptive] If large trees create an additional barrier across the upper part of the street, they can sometimes reduce ventilation.
Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] That means pollutant concentrations near ground level may actually increase under certain conditions.

Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] In a more open street, trees may have different effects because air can move more freely around the vegetation.

Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] It can also move particles towards plant surfaces, increasing deposition.

Lecturer: [clear, matter-of-fact] Their ability to capture particles therefore changes over the seasons.
